title: Research Bite #78: Mixing problems increases performance of all students but especially of low-achieving ones in college calculus
author: Craig Barton
summary: In this edition of his weekly Research Bites, Craig Barton breaks down a study by Steve Bennoun, Veronica Yan and Alice Xu on interleaved homework in a large UCLA calculus course. Two sections of 585 students did identical problems, either blocked by topic or mixed and spread across several weekly assignments, and then swapped halfway through the term. Interleaved homework was linked to higher final exam scores for everyone, with the largest gains for students who had scored lower on the midterm or had weaker prior maths preparation. Barton turns this into four classroom moves: keep old topics returning each week, give lower attainers mixed practice too, train students to choose the method a question needs, and explain why mixed homework feels harder. He closes with honest cautions, since students were not randomly assigned, the study covers one university course, and exam questions resembled the homework.
points: Reordering the same questions so that each topic returns across several weeks, rather than changing the questions themselves, was associated with higher final exam scores.
Struggling students gained the most from interleaving, which undercuts the worry that mixed practice overwhelms those who find the subject hard.
A practical routine is to keep a few questions on the new topic and add one or two from each of the last few weeks, spread through the set and never adjacent.
The proposed mechanism is that blocked homework reveals the method before students read the question, whereas mixed practice makes them decide for themselves, as exams do.
Teachers should tell students that mixed questions are meant to feel harder, so the extra difficulty is not read as a sign that something has gone wrong.
quotes: Mixing up homework questions, so each assignment covers several topics and each topic returns over the following weeks, was linked to higher final exam scores for all students, with the biggest gains for those who were struggling. The only change was the order of the same questions.
Interleaving’s benefits are well established, notably in Doug Rohrer’s school maths trials. Less clear was who gains most, and earlier studies gave mixed answers.

In the study, once a topic had been taught, a question on it appeared on each of the next three weekly homeworks, and two questions on the same topic never sat next to each other. You can do this with questions you already have.
A common worry is that mixed-up questions will overwhelm students who find maths hard. In this study, those students gained the most.

The authors’ explanation (which they flag as a hypothesis they didn’t directly test) is that blocked homework tells students the method before they’ve read the question, whereas exams mix everything up. Mixed practice makes students decide for themselves.
Research elsewhere has found that learners tend to feel mixed practice is going worse than blocked practice, even when they are learning more from it.

Students weren’t randomly assigned, and the sections differed from the start. The study covered a single US university course, and exam questions resembled the homework, so performance on unfamiliar question types is untested.
